Welcome toAll Hallows School
A nurturing 'Home-from-Home' community, proudly supporting local Day School and Nursery families, Military Boarders and International students.
Welcome to All Hallows, where a child's happiness and wellbeing are the absolute foundation of an exceptional education. We are passionately committed to nurturing the whole child, and everything else from academic excellence to character development, flows from this core belief.
This commitment creates a nurturing 'home-from-home' community where every child is truly seen, known, and valued. As a result of our approach, our girls and boys, from Nursery to Year 8, develop into something very special: resilient, reflective individuals who love learning, give their very best, and leave knowing precisely who they are.
Set within 40 acres of beautiful Somerset countryside, our learning environment is expansive. Passionate and engaging class teaching drives our academic life, complemented by outstanding opportunities that lie both inside and outside the classroom: immersive outdoor learning in our extensive 9-acre Forest School, an ambitious Sports programme, and state-of-the-art facilities like our Creative Design Centre for Art, Design & Technology, State-of-the-Art Astro Turf, and bespoke Early Years setting.

Nurturing Creative Thinking in Children: Balancing Tech and Real-World Experiences
Creative thinking helps children respond flexibly to everyday challenges and prepares them for a workplace that values original ideas and adaptability. But how can we nurture the art of creativity in a highly digital world?
Creativity and critical thinking are key skills for increasingly digitalised societies, yet many parents feel uncertain about what creativity actually means or how to develop it.
Understanding how to balance screen time with hands-on play, knowing which digital activities spark imagination and learning to ask the right questions can help your child become a creative thinker. As a prep school focused on nurturing our students’ creativity, we’re here to show you practical ways to support your child’s creative development whilst navigating the digital world together.
Cultivating creative thinking in a digital age
Children need both structured guidance and freedom to explore as they develop creative and critical thinking abilities. Understanding how creativity develops in the brain, providing hands-on experiences with real materials and creating balanced learning spaces all work together to strengthen young minds.
Defining creative and critical thinking for young minds
Creative thinking involves generating new ideas, making connections between different concepts and finding original solutions to problems. It’s the ability to look at situations from multiple angles and imagine possibilities that don’t yet exist.
Critical thinking skills help children analyse information, ask questions and make reasoned decisions. When your child evaluates whether something makes sense or considers different options before choosing, they’re using critical thinking. These skills work alongside creative thinking to help children navigate challenges.
Both thinking styles complement each other in important ways. Creative sparks generate ideas whilst critical thinking helps children evaluate which ideas work best. Young children naturally use both when they engage in pretend play or solve everyday problems. Your role involves providing opportunities for both types of thinking to grow.
The combination of creative and critical thinking builds problem-solving abilities that children will use throughout their lives. These skills help with social-emotional development as children learn to understand different perspectives and manage complex situations.
The science behind creativity: brain development and artistic intelligence
The prefrontal cortex, located at the front of the brain, plays a central role in creative thought and artistic intelligence. This brain region continues developing into early adulthood and handles planning, imagination and making connections between ideas. When children engage in creative activities, they strengthen neural pathways in this area.
Your child’s brain develops through repeated experiences and practice. Each time your child tries a new creative activity or solves a problem in an original way, their brain forms new connections. These pathways become stronger with regular use, making creative thinking easier over time.
Blue sky thinking, aka the ability to imagine without constraints, relies on the brain’s capacity to combine stored information in novel ways. Research shows that varied experiences give children more mental material to work with when generating creative ideas. The more diverse learning experiences they have, the more creative power they can develop.
Physical activity and creative outlets both support healthy brain development. Movement increases blood flow to the brain, whilst artistic activities engage multiple brain regions simultaneously. This combination helps build the cognitive flexibility children need for both creative and critical thinking.
Nurturing creativity through hands-on and authentic activities
Process art focuses on the experience of creating rather than producing a perfect final product. This approach lets children explore materials freely without worrying about making mistakes. Oil pastels, chalk pastels, plasticine clay and natural materials all offer different textures and possibilities for creative expression.
Materials matter when it comes to sparking imagination. Wood scraps, masking tape and items from the natural world provide open-ended possibilities, with the added bonus of exposing children to mind-boosting nature. These authentic materials let children build, construct and create based on their own ideas rather than following predetermined instructions.

You don’t need to structure every moment of your child’s day. Free play and open-ended time allow children to follow their interests without adult direction. During these periods, young children often engage in pretend play that builds both creative thinking and social-emotional development.
Art activities and literacy activities work best when they connect to real experiences. Authentic activities like cooking, gardening or fixing household items teach practical skills while encouraging creative problem-solving. These experiences give children meaningful contexts for learning.

Balancing technology and real-world learning spaces
Learning spaces should include both digital tools and physical materials that encourage hands-on exploration. Your learning environment shapes how children engage with the world around them. A balance between screen time and real-world activities supports healthy development.
The natural world offers learning experiences that technology cannot replicate. Outdoor exploration builds observation skills, encourages curiosity and provides sensory input that screens don’t offer. Regular time outside helps children develop connections to their environment. Students at All Hallows get the opportunity to explore the outdoor environment and benefit from its creativity-boosting nature through our forest school.
Creating balanced learning environments can look something like this:
Art supplies and craft materials
Educational apps with creative features
Building blocks and construction toys
Digital drawing and music creation tools
Books and storytelling props
Age-appropriate coding games
Outdoor exploration areas
Virtual museum tours and nature videos
Interactive learning programmes
Technology works best as one tool amongst many rather than the primary source of entertainment or learning. When you do use digital devices, choose programmes that encourage creativity. Look for apps that let children create, build or solve problems.
Set clear boundaries around screen time to ensure children have ample opportunity for physical play, social interaction and hands-on creative outlets. The goal is to ensure technology benefits your child and doesn’t crowd out other valuable experiences. Young children particularly benefit from tactile, three-dimensional play that builds spatial reasoning and fine motor skills.
Guiding children’s creativity and learning with technology
Technology can be a powerful tool for children’s creativity when parents and educators use it with clear goals and create spaces where young learners can explore, question and build skills that matter in today’s world.
Purposeful integration of educational technologies
Educational technologies work best when you choose them with specific learning goals in mind. Rather than letting children use any app or programme, select tools that encourage creative learning and develop critical thinking skills.
For example, at All Hallows, we give students access to digital devices to enhance their learning through online resources, quizzes and assessments. We recognise the prominence of technology in students’ modern lives, so we focus on making technology educational instead of trying to remove it from our students’ lives.
Look for platforms that let your child create something new instead of just consuming content. Digital art programmes, coding apps and video editing software give children ways to express their ideas and solve problems.
You should match the technology to your child’s age and abilities. A five-year-old needs different tools than a twelve-year-old. Consider using universal design for learning principles when choosing your approach, which means picking options that work for children with different learning styles and needs.
Set clear time limits and purposes for tech use. Tell your child they’ll spend 30 minutes building a digital story or learning basic coding concepts, instead of just mindless scrolling time.
Supporting creative and critical skills at home and school
When children use technology in a meaningful way, they can improve their problem-solving skills and innovation. At home, encourage projects where your child must plan, create and revise their work.
Ask your child to explain their thinking as they work. When they design a character in a digital art programme or solve a puzzle in an educational game, have them talk through their choices.
Create a space where making mistakes is normal and expected, because children enhance their creative thinking through trial and error. When a coding project doesn’t work or a digital design needs changes, help your child see these moments as part of learning.
Open questions and the power of process-driven play
Open questions help children think more deeply about what they’re creating with technology. Instead of asking “Did you finish your project?”, try “What problem are you trying to solve?” or “How did you decide to do it that way?”
These questions shift focus from the final product to the thinking process. When children explain their reasoning and explore different solutions, learning through play with digital technologies is a richer experience.
Let your child take the lead in their digital projects. Process-driven play means valuing exploration over perfect outcomes. When your child experiments with animation software or builds something in a creative app, resist the urge to show them the “right” way immediately.
Give children time to struggle with challenges before stepping in. This builds persistence and creative problem-solving abilities that extend beyond technology use.
Building inclusive and empowering learning environments
An empowering learning environment with technology considers different abilities, interests and cultural backgrounds. Not every child will enjoy the same digital tools or learn the same way.
Offer variety in how your child can use technology creatively. Some children prefer visual arts programmes whilst others like music creation apps or storytelling platforms. Pay attention to what engages your child and build on those interests.
Be aware of how cultural norms and your family’s social system affect technology use. Some families have different values about screen time or digital creation. Find a balance that works for your household whilst still giving your child opportunities to develop digital creativity skills.
Make technology accessible to all children in your care. This might mean adjusting settings for children with different needs or choosing programmes that work with assistive technologies. Create rules and expectations that help rather than limit creative exploration.
Frequently asked questions
Parents today face unique challenges balancing technology with traditional play while nurturing their children’s creative abilities. These questions address practical concerns about screen time limits, creative development activities and age-appropriate digital boundaries.
How can parents encourage creative thinking in children while managing screen time?
Set clear daily limits for recreational screen use based on your child’s age. The key is creating designated tech-free times during meals, before bed and during outdoor play.
Establish specific zones in your home where devices are not allowed. This helps children naturally shift towards physical play, reading and creative activities without constant digital distractions.
Replace passive screen time with interactive digital experiences that require input and decision-making. When children do use technology, choose apps and games that involve creating, building or problem-solving rather than simply watching content.
Monitor what your children access online and participate in their digital activities when possible. Co-viewing and discussing content together helps your child think critically about what they see on screens.
What are the practical benefits of creative arts and play for children’s development in a technology-rich environment?
Hands-on creative activities develop fine motor skills – drawing, painting and sculpting strengthen hand-eye coordination and muscle control needed for writing and other physical tasks.
Technology enhances problem-solving and critical thinking when it’s balanced with traditional play. Children who engage in both digital and physical creative activities show stronger cognitive flexibility.
Arts and crafts provide sensory experiences that are essential for brain development in young children. Touching different textures, mixing colours and manipulating materials creates neural connections that purely digital experiences cannot achieve.
Creative play without screens builds patience and sustained attention. Unlike apps that provide instant feedback, traditional art projects teach children to work through challenges and see ideas through to completion.

Welcome from the Head
A Foundation of Happiness
Welcome to All Hallows, a truly unique and inclusive Somerset Prep School where pupils, parents, and staff alike feel they truly belong.
My journey here spans almost three decades, and the core philosophy has remained unwavering: your child’s happiness and wellbeing are the absolute foundation of everything we do. This focus on creating a secure, supportive environment ensures every child can thrive.
Leading the way in Wellbeing
This commitment to pastoral excellence is not just a promise; it is nationally recognised. I am deeply honoured to have been invited to join the prestigious National Education Panel at the Anna Freud Centre - a world-leading organisation dedicated to improving children’s mental health and wellbeing.
This appointment is a direct reflection of our belief that a great education must nurture the whole child - their curiosity, confidence, creativity, and wellbeing - as much as their academic outcomes. This ensures All Hallows School remains at the forefront of best practices, giving our children the very best foundation to flourish.
Our Whole Child philosophy & outcomes
Believing that the different aspects of a child’s life are mutually reinforcing, we work in close partnership with parents to develop each pupil emotionally, creatively, intellectually, socially, and spiritually. We cultivate essential characteristics like resilience, teamwork, and open-mindedness, believing there are no ceilings to learning.
This distinctive approach is hugely successful:
Our pupils are busy, happy, energetic, and share a love of the outdoor life, with art, creative design, music, and sport offered to everyone.
Each child leave us exceptionally well-prepared for their senior schools of choice. Furthermore, around 65% of our pupils in recent years have achieved a scholarship or award in the process.
The All Hallows Community
We are an entirely inclusive Christian school, warmly welcoming children and families of all faiths and none.
For our boarders, our main house offers a true 'home-from-home' experience a warm and caring atmosphere, complete with log fires and welly boots. This sense of family permeates the whole of our school life.
By proudly joining the Monkton Family of Schools, we share resources and expertise, strengthening our provision while maintaining our unique identity and independence for senior school choices.
I urge you to come and visit so you can experience the genuine warmth and sheer vibrancy of our community in action. I would be delighted to meet you.
Dr Trevor Richards
Headmaster, All Hallows School

About Us
History and Local Information
All Hallows is nestled in the rural Somerset countryside – a great county in which to live. It is situated just seven miles from Frome, a bustling and eclectic market town keen on independence and its sense of community. It was recently named South West Regional Winner of the Sunday Times Guide to the Best Places to Live.
A stone’s throw away is Bruton, a small ancient town listed in the Domesday Book of 1086, well-known on the art scene for the Hauser and Wirth Gallery as well as being home to some fantastic restaurants. Other notable places nearby are the historic spa city of Bath, the vibrant city of Bristol, the free-spirited town of Glastonbury, and Wells, the smallest city in England.
At All Hallows, we place great value on being part of our local community. We take part in events such as the Frome Arts Festival as well as supporting the Bath and West Show and Nunney Horse Trials. We organise community concerts and our choir regularly ventures out to sing in various places including local parish churches.
The UK's seventh biggest county, Somerset has a landscape of rural rolling hills, coastal cliffs, cityscapes and quintessential villages. It is truly a diverse and interesting place to live.
A brief history…
The school was founded by Francis Dix in 1938 in Bognor Regis, with just one pupil. Numbers quickly grew but the outbreak of the Second World War meant safer accommodation was required. This was sought in Devon and, by the summer of 1940, All Hallows was at Scorhill near Chagford where the River Teign, running through the grounds, acted as a bathing-pool and Dartmoor was a magnificent playground. The school remained in Devon until the end of 1945 and relocated to its current home of Cranmore Hall in 1946. Originally a boys' school, All Hallows opened its doors to girls in 1972.
Cranmore, the name, comes from Crane Mere or Lake of the Cranes. This is why the head of a crane forms part of our school logo and why images of cranes can be seen around the school with some particularly fine ones in the Art Department. We were delighted recently when cranes were re-introduced to Somerset.
The main school building, Cranmore Hall, was formerly the home of the Paget family, and has history dating back to the 17th Century when it was owned by the Glastonbury Monks. Like many large country houses during the Second World War, it was put to very good use, perhaps unusually though, as a maternity hospital.

A parent’s perspective of life at All Hallows
Welcome to the All Hallows School Podcast, the place where we talk to staff, parents and pupils to find out more about life at the school.
In this episode we’re talking to Katharine Cameron Clarke, parent to two daughters aged 12 and 14 both of whom have gone through the school years at All Hallows. We’re going to talk about finding the right school for her children and why the family stuck with All Hallows, what the boarding experience is like at the school, and the opportunities the girls both received in their time at the school.
Katharine also breaks down the stigma surrounding independent education with her own personal experience. So come with me as we talk to Katharine Cameron Clarke.

pageCache.text:
What To Actually Look For On A Prep School Open Day
A Family’s Guide To Feeling Truly At Home
Walking into a school for the first time can feel overwhelming, with polished brochures and a busy schedule pulling your attention in every direction. What To Actually Look For On A Prep School Open Day goes beyond the glossy prospectus and into the small, everyday details that show what life is really like for a child there. Wellies lined up by the door, children greeting visitors with confidence, or a log fire in the hall on a cold morning can tell you more than any set of exam results ever could.
Choosing a school is a team effort involving the whole family, and open days give you the chance to see whether your child would truly belong there, not just achieve there. Whether you’re visiting during open-day season for a single Open Morning or working your way through several Open Events and Open Houses, it helps to know what you’re actually looking for before you arrive.
This article walks you through the details worth paying attention to, so you leave each visit with a clear sense of whether your child would be seen, known and valued, rather than just another name on a list.
Preparing Your Family’s Visit
A good open day starts before you arrive. A little planning around booking, questions and logistics means you and your child get more out of the time you spend on site.
Book Early and Read the Admissions Details
Open days fill up quickly, especially for popular year groups, so book your place as soon as dates are announced. You’ll usually find these on the school website or shared through the school’s social media pages.
Before you go, take a proper look at the admissions process and admissions policy. This gives you a sense of how places are offered, what the school values, and whether your child fits the entry criteria.
Make a note of the application deadline too, as some schools ask families to register interest well before the actual visit. If anything is unclear, the admissions team will usually answer questions by phone or email ahead of time.
Bring the Right Questions for Your Child
Your child’s experience of the day matters just as much as yours. Involve them in preparing a few questions of their own, whether that’s about clubs, friendship groups or what a typical day looks like.
As a family, think about what you want to know beyond the basics. School Atlas suggests covering teaching, pastoral care and SEND support if these are relevant to you, alongside logistical questions about results and daily routines.
It helps to write your questions down beforehand, as it’s easy to forget them once you’re being shown around. Choosing a school is a team effort involving the whole family, so ask your child what they’d like to see or ask before you set off.
Bring a notebook so you can jot down answers, since most schools show several families around on the same day and details can blur together afterwards.
Plan Travel, Timing and Practicalities
Work out your route and parking in good time, particularly if the school is somewhere you haven’t visited before. Some open days run on a timetable with set slots, so check whether you need to arrive at a specific time or if you can drop in.
If transport is a factor in your decision, ask about local transport providers and whether the school offers minibus routes from nearby towns.
It’s also worth checking what happens after your visit. Many schools use a parent portal to share follow-up information, offer letters or additional resources once you’ve registered interest.
If you’re weighing up more than one school, sites such as Talk Education and School Search can help you compare options and keep track of open day dates across different schools.
The Feeling of Belonging and Everyday Care
The way staff greet your child in the corridor tells you more than any prospectus ever could. Watch closely, ask direct questions, and you’ll get a real sense of whether this is a place where your child could truly belong.
Notice How Children Are Welcomed and Spoken To
Watch how staff greet pupils as they pass by. Do teachers know names, or is it a polite nod to a stranger?
A school where children are seen and known will show it in small moments. Look out for a member of staff crouching down to speak to a young child at their level, or a teacher remembering what a pupil said last week.
These little signs matter more than a rehearsed welcome speech. You can notice these details by paying attention during your tour rather than just listening to what staff tell you.
Also notice how older pupils speak to younger ones. Kindness between year groups often says more about the culture than anything an adult tells you.
Ask How Pastoral Support Works in Practice
Pastoral care sounds good on paper, but you need to know how it actually works day to day. Ask who your child would go to if they felt worried, left out, or unwell.
Find out if there’s a form tutor, house parent, or key member of staff responsible for wellbeing. Ask how SEN leaders support children with additional needs, and how staff spot problems before they grow.
Questions worth asking:
These practical details show whether pastoral care is a genuine system or just a phrase in the prospectus.
Check Inclusion, Friendships and Settling In
Ask how the school helps new children settle in, especially if they join partway through the year. Many schools use buddy systems, where an existing pupil is paired with a newcomer to help them find their feet.
Ask about induction programmes too. A good induction should cover more than just where the toilets are. It should help a child understand routines, make friends, and feel part of the group within the first few weeks.
Whether you’re looking at a prep school, or a private day or boarding school, ask how staff support children who find friendships tricky. Find out how the school includes children from different backgrounds, family setups, or needs, whether that’s day pupils, boarders, or children from military or international families.
You should ask how children are matched with buddies and how staff check in on new starters after the first few weeks, not just on day one.
Learning, Spaces and Life Beyond the Classroom
Your child’s day involves far more than lessons in a classroom. Look closely at teaching, at the spaces where creativity happens, and at the small daily routines that make up school life, because these show whether your child will truly feel at home.
Look Beyond Displays to Teaching and Learning
Wall displays and tidy classrooms look lovely, but they don’t tell you how your child will actually learn. Ask to see a real lesson in progress, not just a staged demonstration for visitors.
Watch how teachers speak to pupils. Do they know names? Do they seem genuinely interested in each child, not just the class as a whole?
It’s worth asking how the school prepares older pupils for Common Entrance or other senior school exams. Many schools follow guidance set by the Independent Schools Examinations Board, so ask how your child’s progress and exam entries are recorded and communicated to you.
You should also ask about learning support and how the school helps children who find certain subjects difficult, as well as those who need extra stretch.
Explore Creative, Outdoor and Co-Curricular Opportunities
A good prep school offers far more than academic lessons. Visit the music department, the DT department and the art studio to see whether pupils’ own work is genuinely on show, not just neatly framed examples.
Ask what extracurricular activities and hobbies are on offer beyond the timetable. Clubs, sports and creative pursuits often shape a child’s happiest school memories.
If the school has a Forest School, ask how often your child would take part and what it actually involves. Muddy boots and outdoor learning often say more about a school’s values than any prospectus photo.
Consider Routines, Food, Travel and Boarding
Small daily details matter just as much as academic results. Ask what a typical day looks like, from morning drop-off to home time, and how the school communicates any changes to you as a family.
Find out about food. Is there a varied menu, and can staff cater for allergies or family preferences?
If you’re considering boarding, ask about evening routines, weekend activities and how homesick children are supported.
Practical matters count too. Ask about transport providers if your child needs a school bus, and how the school’s security service keeps pupils safe throughout the day.
Deciding Whether the School Is the Right Fit
Once your visit is over, take a step back and look at the whole picture. This means weighing up what you saw against what you were promised, understanding the practical steps ahead, and bringing your child into the conversation before you commit.
Compare What You Saw With What Was Promised
Before your visit, you probably looked at the school website and its social media pages. These will have painted a picture of school life, from the classrooms to the clubs on offer.
Now is the time to check if that picture matched reality. Did the pupils seem genuinely happy, or just well-rehearsed for visitors? Did the “seen, known and valued” feeling the school talks about actually come through when you spoke to staff and pupils?
Look for small, specific details rather than vague impressions. Wellies lined up neatly by the door or a warm welcome from a Year 6 pupil showing you round says more than a glossy brochure ever could.
Write down your first impressions while they’re still fresh. You’ll want to compare these notes if you visit more than one school.
Clarify Entry Requirements and Financial Questions
Before you go any further, get clear answers on the admissions process. Ask the Admissions Team to walk you through the entrance exam procedure, including what admissions tests are used and when they take place.
Some schools test general ability, others focus on English and maths, so it’s worth knowing exactly what your child will face. If your child is due to start in Year 6, ask whether entry at that stage is more competitive than other year groups.
Money matters too, so don’t be shy about asking directly. Get clear figures on:
Getting these answers early means fewer surprises later.
Tuition costs for each year group
Involve Your Child Before Taking the Next Step
Choosing a school is a team effort involving the whole family, not just a decision made on your child’s behalf. Once you’ve gathered the facts, sit down with your child and ask what they thought.
Did they enjoy the visit? Did they picture themselves there? Their answer matters, even if the final decision rests with you.
Talk through what stood out to them, whether it was a particular teacher, a sports hall, or the log fires in the entrance hall. These small details often stick with children more than exam results.
If you’re still unsure, it’s worth arranging a second visit or asking to speak with current parents. A school that truly wants your child to belong will be happy to help you feel confident before you take the next step, as outlined in this prep school checklist for open mornings.
Frequently Asked Questions
Every family walks into an open day with a slightly different list of worries and priorities, from whether your child will settle in to whether the academic pace is right for them. Below are the questions that come up again and again, answered simply so you know exactly what to look and
What should we look for in the classrooms, boarding houses and shared spaces on a visit?
Step into a real lesson if you’re able to, not just a demonstration set up for visitors. You want to see how pupils behave and speak when they think no one important is watching.
Ask about class sizes and how work is set for children who are ahead or need extra support. This gives you a clearer picture of daily teaching than exam results alone.
If boarding is part of the offer, ask to see the actual dormitories and common rooms rather than just the entrance hall. Checking the atmosphere, meeting staff and asking questions face to face tells you far more than any website description.
Notice the little details in shared spaces, such as children’s artwork on the walls or comfortable reading corners. These show whether a school has been genuinely lived in by its pupils, not just tidied for the day.
Which questions will help us understand the school’s academic standards and support?
Ask for specific figures rather than general claims. A school that can tell you exam pass rates, scholarship numbers or destination schools by name is being upfront with you.
Find out what qualifications the teaching staff hold and how long most of them have stayed at the school. Long-serving staff often signal a settled, well-supported team.
Ask how the school supports children who need extra help, as well as those who need extra stretch. Understanding daily life for pupils matters more than headline results when you’re picturing your own child there.
Don’t be afraid to ask about homework loads and how much support parents are expected to give at home. This helps you judge whether the pace suits your family’s routine.
How do pupils, parents and staff speak to one another during an open day?
Listen closely to the tone used around the school, not just the words. Warm, easy exchanges between staff and pupils usually reflect how the school runs day to day.
Notice whether pupils leading tours speak confidently and naturally, rather than reciting a script. This often shows how much trust the school places in its older children.
Pay attention to how staff speak about parents too. You want to feel like part of a genuine partnership, whether you’re a day family, a boarding family, a military family or an international family joining from overseas.

pageCache.text:
Wellbeing and Learning: Why the Connection Should Come as No Surprise
I recently read the Times Educational Supplement whitepaper, Learning and wellbeing in schools, with a mixture of both encouragement and surprise. Encouragement because its central argument deserves attention—that learning and wellbeing belong at the heart of the same conversation. Surprise because this is presented as a “new perspective”.
At All Hallows, that connection has long been one of the principles on which our provision is built. As a Head and a psychologist, I find it difficult to imagine approaching children’s learning and development in any other way.
A False Dichotomy in Education
The whitepaper describes a persistent separation between academic learning and wellbeing across education. It even acknowledges that the authors’ own survey asked schools to choose between wellbeing and academic outcomes when identifying their priorities. That seems a revealing question. Why should schools be choosing?
A child anxious about making mistakes may avoid contributing. A pupil who feels overlooked may gradually stop asking for help. Equally, understanding a difficult concept, receiving thoughtful feedback or discovering an unexpected strength or passion can cultivate a child’s confidence and sense of themselves. The relationship works in both directions.
A “Future” Vision Already in Practice
The paper includes a contribution from Louka Parry, described as an “Education Futurist”, who challenges the separation of learning and wellbeing. His argument is welcome. Nevertheless, I found myself wondering whether this particular vision of the future might look familiar to families already at All Hallows. Children being known, valued and feeling that they belong has been central to our thinking for a considerable time.
Embedding Wellbeing into Daily Classroom Life
One of the whitepaper’s most useful observations is that effective teaching and effective support for wellbeing share a common ground. It highlights trusting, warm relationships, clear expectations, meaningful feedback and opportunities for pupils to have a voice in their learning. These are practical features of any safe and effective classroom, experienced through numerous ordinary interactions throughout the day.
That matters because wellbeing can otherwise become another initiative squeezed into an already busy timetable. The paper rightly questions the sustainability of continually adding separate responsibilities for teachers. A timetabled lesson has value, but its influence depends on what happens around it. To be truly powerful and effective, this thinking needs to be part of a school’s culture and DNA.
Building Resilience Through Productive Challenge
Taking wellbeing seriously does not mean removing every difficulty. Children need appropriate challenge, opportunities to struggle productively and adults who help them recognise what they might do next to move forward. Feeling supported makes those experiences more manageable; overcoming them can be deeply rewarding. It can be difficult to gain self-efficacy and resilience if we never face difficulties, and that applies across a child’s life, not just in the classroom.
Looking Forward
No school is perfect and we have plenty still to learn ourselves, yet there is quiet reassurance in seeing a proposed direction for education reflected in principles already embedded at All Hallows. I wholeheartedly welcome the acknowledgement that wellbeing and learning are inextricably linked. My raised eyebrow is reserved for the suggestion that this should still be a revelation!

pageCache.pageTitle: AI, learning and the value of doing the hard bit | All Hallows, Somerset
pageCache.text:
AI, learning and the value of doing the hard bit
One of the most interesting discussions I have been part of this week was at a symposium of heads and Ed Tech consultants exploring the use of AI in schools, and what it might mean for children and their learning. It was fascinating because it was not really a conversation about technology at all. It was a debate about what we think education is for.
The panel repeatedly returned to character development, values, relationships, curiosity and the cultivation of independent thinkers. The fundamental question was therefore not simply, “What can AI do?”, but “What do we want children to become, and what experiences help them get there?”
Beyond the Final Output
For me, using AI to do the thinking for a child is a bit like taking a forklift to the gym.
Now, I quite like going to the gym, and if I drove a forklift in, picked up the weights, moved them from the floor to the rack and drove home again, I would technically have completed the task. The weights would have moved from A to B, but I would have rather missed the point.
I do not go to the gym because I have a need to move heavy objects around. I go to become fitter and stronger, to maintain my mobility, to unwind after a busy day, and because I enjoy seeing some friendly faces and being part of a community. Moving the weights is simply the means through which those things happen.
The True Process of Learning
Learning is remarkably similar. When a child writes an essay, the finished essay is not the whole point. They have to recall what they know, find the words, decide what they think, structure their ideas and occasionally realise that something does not make sense and have another go.
The same is true in mathematics. Unpicking a question, remembering a method, applying it, getting stuck, spotting where something has gone wrong and trying again are all part of developing understanding.
Producing Something vs. Learning Something
AI is extraordinarily good at getting the weight from the floor to the rack. It can produce the essay, solve the problem and find the words, but if the child has outsourced their thinking, what have they gained? They may have produced a better piece of work, but they have not necessarily become a better writer, or developed the confidence to work something out for themselves.
That distinction matters, and we must not confuse producing something with learning something.
The Joy of the Struggle
Sometimes the difficult bit, the struggle, is the important bit. Wrestling with something, making mistakes and eventually reaching that lovely moment of, “Ah, I get it now,” is often precisely where the learning happens. Thinking hard is when learning is at its most exciting, too.
So, the question for schools is not simply, “Can AI do this?” Increasingly, the answer will be yes. The more important question is, “If AI does this for the child, what does the child no longer get to do?”
Our Approach at All Hallows
Hence, our approach at All Hallows is not anti-technology, but it remains pro-learning, pro-thinking and very firmly pro-children. We will continue to engage with and understand AI, and think carefully alongside parents about its place in education.
For now, however, when it comes to the core business of children learning, we are quite happy for them to do the heavy lifting themselves.

How to Develop Quiet Confidence in Introverted Children
Introverted children are often misunderstood by their parents, who mistake their quiet nature for shyness. Many parents worry when their child prefers quiet time alone or takes longer to warm up in social situations, but these traits reflect a thoughtful individual who processes their world in their own unique way.
Introverted children can develop strong confidence by honouring their inner world whilst building skills to navigate social situations comfortably. Understanding how your child processes experiences helps you create the right balance between respecting their need for calm spaces and gently encouraging growth.
Here, we’ll explore the specific needs of introverted kids and share practical approaches to support their development. You’ll learn how to recognise your child’s strengths, create routines that work with their needs and help them build the quiet confidence that comes from being understood and supported.
Understanding the unique needs of introverted children
Introverted children process the world differently than their extroverted peers, requiring parents to recognise these differences and respond with appropriate support. Your child’s need for quiet time, sensitivity to sensory input and rich inner world reflect who they are, and should be nurtured and respected.
Recognising introversion versus shyness and social anxiety
Introversion is a personality trait that you should respect. Introverted children recharge through solitude and prefer deeper connections with fewer friends. This differs significantly from shyness or social anxiety, which involve fear or discomfort in social situations, but the two are often conflated.
Shy children want social connection but feel nervous about it, while children with social anxiety experience intense fear that interferes with daily life. Introverted children, however, simply find too much external stimulation draining and need time alone to restore their energy.
Introverted children process information more deeply and reflect before acting. They manage their energy and choose meaningful interactions over constant socialising, which can be wrongly perceived as avoiding socialisation because of shyness or fear.
How introverted children experience the world
Introverted children have a rich inner world filled with thoughts, ideas and imagination. They process experiences internally before sharing them with others, which means they often need time to think before responding to questions or making decisions.
Introverted children thrive in calm, consistent yet enriching environments. They dislike sudden changes to their schedules and intrusions into their space, preferring reliable periods of quiet time to process their thoughts, beliefs and feelings.
In the school system, introverted children may struggle with constant group work and high-energy environments. They learn best through observation and independent work. They need time to warm up to new teachers, classmates and activities rather than jumping in immediately.
The role of environment and sensory input
Introverted children are often more sensitive to sensory input than extroverted children. Bright lights, loud noises, crowded spaces and busy schedules can overwhelm them quickly. Your child’s nervous system processes stimulation more thoroughly, which means they reach their limit faster.
Common environmental triggers include:
Introverted children need a calm home environment where they can retreat and recharge. After school or social events, they require downtime in their own space to process the day’s experiences, which is how they balance their day.
Understanding attachment theory helps explain why your introverted child may take longer to separate from you in new situations. They need a secure base before exploring unfamiliar environments.
noisy classrooms or playgrounds
multiple activities in one day
large birthday parties or family gatherings
shopping centres or busy public spaces
unexpected changes to routine.
Celebrating introverted children’s gifts and strengths
Introverted children possess unique strengths that deserve recognition and celebration. These children often demonstrate deep thinking, creativity, empathy and strong observation skills.
Key strengths of introverted children:
Introverted children tend to excel in independent projects, creative pursuits and one-on-one conversations. They bring curiosity, compassion and careful attention to their interests and relationships.
Building character in your introverted child means celebrating these quiet strengths rather than pushing them to become more outgoing. Their attentive, thoughtful way of engaging with the world is valuable exactly as it is and doesn’t need to be changed.
Creative problem-solving: their inner world fuels imagination.
Meaningful relationships: they form deep, lasting connections.
Practical strategies for supporting quiet confidence
Building quiet confidence in introverted kids requires specific approaches at home and school, teaching social skills without overwhelming them and providing tools to handle stress and anxiety management techniques effectively.
Creating a supportive environment
Your home should offer spaces for regular quiet time where your introverted child can recharge after social interaction. Set up a calm space with books, art supplies or other materials for creative expression. This area can be their retreat after school or group activities.
Work with your child’s class teacher to understand classroom dynamics. Request that they avoid singling out your child in front of others or labelling them as shy publicly. Your child’s class teacher can help by pairing your child with one classmate during group work rather than placing them in large teams, or implementing more independent work.
During summer holidays, maintain structure while allowing downtime. Balance social connections with restoration periods so your child doesn’t become overwhelmed by constant activity.
Nurturing social skills without pressure
Start small with social skills development. Arrange one-on-one play dates before expecting your child to manage birthday parties or team sport events. Single friendships allow introverted kids to practise conversation and develop listening skills without the chaos of group settings.
Introduce small talk through role play at home. Practise greetings, asking questions and responding to common scenarios. These rehearsals reduce social awkwardness when real situations arise.
Consider activities that suit your child’s temperament:
Avoid pushing team sport participation if it causes distress. Not every child thrives in competitive group environments, and that’s fine.
Encouraging self-expression and self-esteem
Teach positive affirmations to counter imposter syndrome and negative self-talk. Instead of “I can’t do this,” encourage phrases like “I can try this” or “My quiet nature is a strength.” Reinforcing this daily will help your child understand that their personality traits are positive.
You can support your child’s self-expression through various outlets, including:
Celebrate mistakes as learning opportunities. When your child fears failure, they avoid trying new things. Show them that everyone makes errors, and these moments help us grow.
Avoid comparing your introverted child to siblings or peers, especially regarding social expectations. Comments like “Why can’t you be more like your brother?” damage self-esteem and suggest something is wrong with them.
journaling private thoughts
creating art without needing to explain it
writing stories or poetry
playing musical instruments
building or making things.
Addressing social challenges and coping techniques
Equip your child with specific coping skills for overwhelming situations. Teach them a simple breathing technique: breathe in for four counts, hold for four, breathe out for four. This calms the nervous system during stressful social environments.
Help them develop exit strategies for when group activities become too much. Agree on signals they can use at school or social events to indicate they need a break. Taking brief walks or visiting the toilet provides legitimate quiet moments.
Prepare your child for common scenarios:
Group work at school
Ask to work with one partner first
Arrive early before crowds build
Practise at home multiple times
Find one friendly teammate to stick with
Address social and emotional challenges by validating your child’s feelings. When they express anxiety about social situations, listen without immediately problem-solving. Sometimes they need acknowledgement that these situations are genuinely difficult.
Teach them that declining invitations is acceptable. They don’t need to attend every party or join every club to be valued. Quality social connections matter more than quantity.
Work together on confident responses to common questions. Write out responses to questions like “Why are you so quiet?” Your child might say, “I prefer listening” or “I think before I speak.” Having prepared answers reduces anxiety when these questions arise.
Frequently asked questions
Parents often struggle to distinguish introversion from other traits and wonder how to support their child without changing who they are. These questions address the specific challenges of recognising introversion, building confidence and bridging communication gaps between different personality types.
What are the most common signs that a child is introverted rather than shy or anxious?
Introverted children recharge through alone time and prefer quieter environments. They might spend time in their room after school or social events because they need to recover their energy.
These children often think carefully before speaking and prefer one-on-one conversations over group discussions. They show deep focus on specific interests and can spend hours engaged in solitary activities like reading, drawing or building.
The key difference lies in fear versus preference. Shyness involves fear of negative social evaluation, while introversion is simply a preference for less stimulating environments. A shy child wants to join the party but feels held back by worry about judgement. An introverted child may genuinely prefer staying home with a book because that activity is more appealing than the party itself. There’s no fear driving the choice.
Social anxiety shows up differently. A child with social anxiety may ruminate after social events, avoid future gatherings or display physical symptoms of distress. An introverted child will recharge after a draining event and return to their normal baseline.
Watch how your child recovers. If they bounce back after quiet time, you’re seeing introversion. If they continue to show distress or avoidance, they may be socially anxious.
How can parents build an introverted child’s self-esteem without pushing them to be more outgoing?
Confidence in an introverted child looks different from confidence in an extroverted one. You don’t need to turn your child into an extroverted individual, but instead play to their many strengths.
An introverted child shows confidence through sustained focus on complex interests, forming deep friendships with one or two people or holding clear values even when peers push back. These expressions of confidence are just as valid as speaking up in crowds or volunteering for lead roles.
Celebrate depth over volume in your child’s life. Notice when they spend hours building something or think carefully before answering a question. Name these strengths explicitly so they understand their natural way of engaging has value.
Give your child real choices about which activities to pursue, which friendships to invest in and how they spend their downtime – this autonomy builds confidence. A child who feels in control of their own environment develops a stronger internal sense of self.
Let them prepare before social situations. Tell them who will be there, what will happen, how long it will last and when they can have quiet time afterwards. This preparation gives your child the time and space they need to show up fully.
Avoid comparing them to more outgoing children or suggesting they should be different. Even subtle comments about “coming out of their shell” send the message that something about them needs fixing.
How can I support my introverted child in making friends and maintaining friendships?
Introverted children typically prefer fewer, deeper friendships rather than large social circles. You don’t need to change this in your child, but you can help them facilitate these friendships.
Focus on quality over quantity. Help your child identify one or two peers who share their interests or communication style. Arrange shorter, structured playdates rather than long, unstructured group activities.
Side-by-side activities work better than face-to-face socialising for many introverted children. Suggest activities like building with blocks, doing art projects or playing video games where the focus is on the shared activity rather than constant conversation.
Give your child recovery time between social events. Don’t schedule back-to-back playdates or activities. Build in quiet time at home so they can recharge before the next interaction. You should also teach them it’s acceptable to decline invitations or leave events early when they feel drained. This prevents social burnout and helps them maintain the friendships they do have.
Support their preferred methods of communication. Some introverted children find it easier to maintain friendships through messaging or video calls rather than in-person hangouts. Both methods are valid.
Never force your child to hug, kiss or physically interact with friends or family members if they’re uncomfortable. Respecting their boundaries teaches them their physical and emotional limits matter.

What Teams Sport Really Teaches Children Beyond Fitness
When your child joins a team, you might think you are simply signing them up for exercise. But sport for children is about far more than physical activity alone.
The real value comes from what happens between the whistles: your child learning to work with others, cope with setbacks, and understand their place within a group. Team sports and school sports give children a space where they are seen by teammates, coaches, and you as a parent, not just for how fast they run or how many goals they score, but for how they show up for others.
This matters for the whole family, not just the child on the pitch. Watching your child navigate a difficult match or bounce back from a loss can shape how you understand their mental health and character long after the final whistle blows.
Belong, Contribute And Grow Together
When your child joins a team, they learn far more than how to kick a ball or run faster. They pick up social skills, leadership skills, and a real sense of belonging that stays with them long after the final whistle.
Learning Social Skills Through Shared Goals
Your child will not learn to work with others by being told to. They learn it by doing it, week after week, alongside teammates who all want the same thing.
Organised sport gives your child a natural setting to practise talking, listening and compromising. On a football pitch or netball court, there is no time for a long explanation. Your child has to communicate quickly, read the room, and adjust.
These moments add up. Your child learns to cooperate and problem solve with others, which helps them well beyond the sports field. The same skills carry over into classroom group work, family life and, later on, the workplace.
Building Confidence, Empathy And Leadership Skills
Every match brings a mix of wins and losses, and your child will feel both. That mix is where real growth happens.
Watching a teammate struggle and offering support teaches empathy in a way no classroom lesson can. Taking a turn as captain, even for one match, builds leadership skills your child can carry into other parts of life.
Confidence grows slowly, through small moments rather than one big breakthrough. Your child might miss a goal one week and score the winner the next. Over time, they learn that mistakes are not the end of the story, they are part of it.
This steady mix of setback and success helps your child manage stress and boosts their mood, while also giving them the tools to lead, support others, and bounce back when things do not go to plan.
Creating A Positive Sporting Environment
The environment your child plays in matters just as much as the sport itself. A positive sporting environment, one built on fairness, encouragement and respect, shapes how your child sees competition and cooperation for years to come.
Look for sports clubs and community clubs that put this into practise, not just into words. Signs of a good club include:
Groups such as Play by the Rules work to promote fair, safe and inclusive sport across clubs. When your child plays in a setting like this, they learn that being part of a team means being included, valued and treated fairly, both on and off the pitch.
Coaches who praise effort, not just results
Clear rules that apply to everyone equally
Parents encouraged to support rather than pressure
Resilience, Responsibility And Healthy Routines
Team sport gives your child more than fitness. It builds habits and coping skills that carry into everyday life, from handling a tough day to eating well and getting enough rest.
Meeting Setbacks With Perspective
Your child will lose matches, drop catches and sit on the bench sometimes. That’s part of the deal, and it teaches them something maths lessons can’t.
They learn to shake off a bad moment and try again next week. This kind of sporting resilience brings the same mental health benefits as resilience built through family life or friendships.
Over time, your child starts to see a missed goal or a lost game as one moment, not a verdict on who they are. That shift in thinking is one you’ll notice off the pitch too, whether it’s a tricky exam or a falling-out with a friend.
Balancing Commitment, Rest And Healthy Eating
Team sport asks your child to turn up, even when they’d rather stay home. That’s where responsibility starts to take shape.
Alongside commitment, your child needs to learn how to rest and refuel properly. Good health promotion through sport covers healthy eating and sleep, not just training hours.
Here’s what a balanced routine tends to include:
You can help by keeping mealtimes steady and making sure your child isn’t overloaded with back-to-back fixtures.
A consistent bedtime, especially before match days
Supporting Wellbeing Beyond The Playing Field
Regular physical activity improves blood flow and supports better metabolic outcomes, which matters for your child’s long-term health. It’s also one of the clearest tools we have against childhood obesity, a growing concern in public health circles.
But the benefits go further than the body. Team sport gives your child a sense of belonging and structure, which supports their mental health as much as their physical health.
You’ll likely see this show up in small ways at home. Better sleep, a steadier mood, and more willingness to try things that feel difficult at first.
Making Sport Part Of School Life
When your child joins our school, sport becomes a natural part of every week, not just something added on. From the classroom to the playing field, we make sure your child feels part of something, whatever their level of ability.
Purposeful PE Lessons And Sports Coaching
Every child takes part in physical education lessons that are planned to build real skills, not just fill time. Your child will learn the principles of athletics alongside teamwork, coordination and confidence.
Our PE lessons are taught by qualified coaches who know how to bring out the best in each child. Whether your child is a natural athlete or still finding their feet, they’ll get the same warm encouragement.
We believe PE lessons should teach more than technique. They should help your child learn to trust their teammates, bounce back from setbacks, and grow in self-belief.
Opportunities Beyond The Timetable
Sport does not stop when the school bell rings. We offer a full athletic programme that includes:
These physical activity programmes and after-school sports sessions mean your child always has somewhere to belong, even outside lesson time. Our built environment, from the playing fields to the sports hall, is designed to make the most of every session.
Pathways For Every Interest And Ambition
Some children play sport simply because they enjoy it. Others want to push further, and we support both.
For families considering us, you’ll find that promoting sports in schools is something we take seriously, right through to sports scholarships for older pupils with real talent and drive.
As one of many independent schools offering this kind of support, we make sure every child, whatever their ambition, has a genuine pathway to follow.
Frequently Asked Questions
Choosing sport for your child raises real questions about confidence, friendship, resilience and how coaches shape character. Here are the answers you need, drawn from what actually happens on the pitch, the court and the sidelines.
How do team sports help children build confidence and feel that they belong?
When your child pulls on a team shirt, they become part of something bigger than themselves. That sense of belonging grows every time they turn up to training, cheer on a teammate, or celebrate a shared win.
Confidence tends to build quietly, not through grand gestures. A child who struggles to speak up in class might find their voice on the football pitch, calling for the ball or organising a defensive line. This carries over: team sports strengthen decision-making and self-belief in ways that ripple into schoolwork and friendships too.
What life skills do children learn from being part of a sports team?
Your child picks up far more than technique when they join a team. They learn to communicate clearly, manage their time around training and matches, and handle both praise and criticism.
These lessons show up in small, everyday moments:
Research points to team sports supporting cognitive and social-emotional growth alongside the physical benefits you would expect. Your child is not just getting fitter — they are learning how to function well within a group.
How can team sports teach children resilience when things do not go to plan?
Losing a match is uncomfortable, but it is also useful. Your child learns that setbacks are not the end of the story, just part of it.
Missing a penalty, dropping a catch or losing a final all sting in the moment. But sport builds perseverance and resilience precisely because children have to face these moments and keep going. Over time, your child stops seeing failure as something to fear and starts seeing it as something to work through.
Do team sports help children develop friendships and social skills?
Friendships formed on a team often run deeper than those made elsewhere. Your child is working towards a shared goal with these people, which creates a different kind of bond.
Shared training sessions, away matches and post-game debriefs give children regular, low-pressure time together. This consistency helps friendships take root naturally. Team sports also build leadership and critical thinking, skills your child will lean on well beyond their playing days.
How do coaches and teammates help children learn responsibility and respect?
A good coach sets clear expectations, and your child learns to meet them. This might mean arriving prepared, respecting the referee’s decision even when it feels unfair, or supporting a teammate having an off day.
Being part of a team also means your child answers to more than just themselves. If they let their side down, they see the direct impact of that. This kind of accountability, built through essential life skills learned in team sports, tends to translate into how your child behaves at school and at home too.
Why do some children lose interest in sport, and how can families help them stay involved?
Interest can fade for all sorts of reasons. Your child might feel out of their depth, find the pressure of competition unpleasant, or simply prefer another activity as they get older.
You can help by keeping the focus on enjoyment rather than results. Ask your child what they like about their sport, not just how the last match went. If one sport is not working, trying another might reignite their interest — different sports offer different life lessons, so a change of activity does not mean losing the benefits altogether. Your steady encouragement, without pushing too hard, often makes the biggest difference.

How Prep Schools Help You Navigate Private Secondary School Admissions
If you have a specific selective secondary school in mind for your child, one of the best ways to secure their chances of admission is through prep school.
Prep schools specialise in securing places in prestigious senior schools, offering structured guidance and exam preparation that significantly improves their chances of gaining admission to competitive secondary schools.
Unlike standard primary schools, prep schools focus specifically on preparing pupils for entry into private secondary schools at age 13. They understand exactly what these schools look for in applicants.
As a prep school, we’ll explain how preparatory schools support families through every stage of the admissions process. You’ll learn about the specific advantages these schools offer, the step-by-step support they provide and how they help your child stand out in a competitive field.
The prep school advantage in navigating secondary admissions
Prep schools offer structured support throughout the entire secondary transfer process, from understanding entry timelines to completing application forms. They’ll provide your child with expert guidance on entrance exams and interview techniques to help them secure admission into their chosen senior school.
Understanding key entry points and transition years
Prep schools prepare pupils for entry at age 13, which are the main transition points to private secondary education. Year 8 students typically sit Common Entrance exams for 13+ admission.
Your child’s prep school will explain the admissions timetable for each pathway. Registration deadlines often fall 18 to 24 months before actual entry. Assessment dates for Common Entrance exams are in November, January, May or June of Year 8.
Understanding these key stages helps you plan ahead. Schools with feeder relationships may offer guaranteed progression routes or priority consideration. Your prep school staff will clarify which entry point suits your child’s development and which secondary schools align with their academic profile.
Guidance through the private school application process
Prep schools manage the administrative aspects of secondary school admissions alongside families. Staff can help you complete application forms accurately and submit them by deadline. They’ll provide clear admissions information about each school’s requirements and oversubscription criteria.
Your prep school can advise on realistic school preferences based on your child’s academic performance and personal qualities. This guidance helps you make an informed decision rather than applying to unsuitable schools.
Many prep schools maintain close relationships with multiple secondary schools. These connections mean staff understand what each institution values in candidates. They’ll help you navigate online application portals and ensure all supporting documentation reaches schools on time.
Support with entrance exams and interview preparation
Prep schools follow a curriculum designed for the Common Entrance, giving your child targeted academic preparation. Teachers will deliver lessons that build the study skills and subject knowledge required for these assessments.
Your child will receive practice papers under timed conditions, helping them prepare effectively for their admissions tests. Staff identify weak areas and provide additional support before assessment dates.
Mock interviews help your child articulate their interests and respond confidently to questions. Teachers can provide feedback on body language, clarity of speech and how to showcase their strengths. This rehearsal reduces anxiety and leads to positive outcomes during actual admissions interviews.
Personalised advice for school preferences and selection
Prep school staff know your child’s academic abilities, personality and interests through daily contact. This knowledge allows them to recommend secondary schools where your child will thrive. They’ll discuss whether day or boarding options suit your family circumstances.
Teachers can arrange visits to potential schools and accompany you when appropriate. They’ll help you evaluate factors like:
When you receive your school place offer through an offer letter, your prep school will help you understand any conditions attached. They’ll support communication with your chosen secondary school through key stage 4 to ensure smooth transition.
academic rigour and setting arrangements
pastoral care systems and house structures
co-curricular opportunities matching your child’s interests
distance and transport logistics.
Step-by-step support throughout the admissions journey
Prep schools guide families through each stage of secondary school admissions, from submitting your initial enquiry form to supporting on appeals. They help parents meet application deadlines and understand admissions arrangements for different school types.
Initial enquiry and open day visits
Your child’s prep school will help you identify suitable secondary schools based on their abilities and interests. They can provide contact details for admissions teams and help you complete enquiry forms for multiple schools.
Prep schools like All Hallows maintain relationships with admissions teams at top independent schools. This means they can advise you on the best school visiting dates and what to expect during open days. They’ll also explain each school’s admissions arrangements, helping you with the application process.
Application rounds and meeting deadlines
Prep schools can help you track application deadlines for all your chosen schools. They can ensure you submit forms on time, whether you apply online or through paper applications.
Different school types have different timelines. Your prep school will know when to register for independent school entrance exams. They’ll help you understand the allocation of school places and how late applications affect your chances.
Key deadlines typically include:
independent school entrance exams (January or February)
scholarship applications (often earlier than standard applications)
Assessment, taster days and transition support
Prep schools will prepare your child for entrance assessments through targeted teaching and progress monitoring. They’ll analyse examination results to identify areas needing improvement and track pupil behaviour to ensure your child presents well during school visits.
Many schools offer taster days where your child spends time at the secondary school. Your child’s prep school will often coordinate these visits and prepare your child for what to expect.
The transition support service at prep schools includes pastoral care and practical preparation. Staff help your child understand new routines, such as school transport policy and school travel assistance options. They also communicate with secondary school admissions teams about your child’s progress and any special circumstances.
Managing offers, waiting lists and appeals
Once your child starts to receive offers, their prep school can help you evaluate options and make informed decisions. They can explain acceptance procedures and deposit requirements for independent schools, as well as the allocation of secondary school places for state schools.
If your child is placed on a waiting list, their prep school can advise on next steps. They’ll help you decide whether to accept another offer while remaining on the list for your preferred school.
Should you need to appeal a decision, your child’s prep school can provide supporting evidence such as assessment data and teacher reports. They can draft letters highlighting your child’s suitability for the school and any exceptional circumstances.
Frequently asked questions
Prep schools offer structured support throughout the admissions journey, from selecting appropriate schools to preparing for assessments and interviews. Understanding how they navigate these challenges helps families make informed decisions about their child’s education.
What advantages does a prep school provide when preparing for selective secondary school entry?
Prep schools give pupils access to small class sizes and individualised attention that builds strong academic foundations. Teachers know each child’s strengths and areas for development, allowing them to tailor preparation for specific entrance requirements.
Prep schools like All Hallows provide rigorous academics alongside enriched opportunities in arts, sports and leadership. This well-rounded education develops the skills that selective secondary schools look for beyond test scores.
The structured environment helps pupils develop good study habits and time management skills. These abilities prove essential when managing the demands of entrance exams and maintaining academic performance during the application period.
How do prep schools support pupils with entrance exams, interviews and assessment days?
Prep schools prepare students with secondary school admissions through assessments, visits and mock interviews. Teachers prepare pupils for cognitive ability tests and standardised assessments that many independent secondary schools now use. This preparation happens within the regular curriculum, making it a part of everyday school life.
Prep schools conduct mock interviews to help pupils feel confident during actual admissions interviews. Staff can provide feedback on communication skills, body language and how to discuss interests and achievements naturally.
Taster days and school visits form part of the preparation process. Pupils learn what to expect during assessment days and how to demonstrate their abilities in unfamiliar settings.
What criteria do independent secondary schools typically use when making admissions decisions?
Independent secondary schools will look at exam results, performance in interviews and students’ school reports. Academic performance remains a primary factor, assessed through entrance exams, pre-tests or cognitive ability tests.
Personal interviews allow admissions staff to understand how well a child might fit within their school community. Schools assess qualities such as curiosity, resilience and enthusiasm for learning during these conversations.
References and school reports provide insight into a pupil’s character, work ethic and behaviour. Many schools consider how pupils contribute to school life through activities, leadership roles and relationships with peers.
Some schools evaluate creative or practical skills through portfolio submissions or practical assessments. These might include art portfolios, musical auditions or sports trials depending on the school’s focus.
How can a prep school advise families on choosing the right independent secondary schools to apply to?
Prep schools can discuss secondary school options with parents, create shortlists and use their relationships with selective schools to support applications. Initial conversations about secondary schools typically begin in Year 5, starting with casual discussions about geography, co-educational or single-sex options and boarding or day preferences. The head or senior staff member guides parents through these early considerations based on their knowledge of each child.
Prep schools help families create realistic shortlists based on their child’s abilities and needs. Teachers can identify whether a child would thrive at particular schools or struggle to keep pace with the academic demands.
Schools draw on their relationships with multiple secondary schools to understand what each looks for in applicants. Prep schools typically feed to numerous different schools and maintain regular communication with their admissions teams.
Staff advise on practical matters such as registration deadlines, which vary significantly between schools. Some schools close applications at the end of Year 5, whilst others remain open later in Year 6.
What role do references, reports and predicted attainment play in secondary school admissions, and how does a prep school help?
References provide secondary schools with detailed information about a pupil’s academic progress, character and potential. Prep school teachers write these references with knowledge of both the pupil and what the receiving school values.
School reports demonstrate consistent performance and attitude over time. These documents show how pupils engage with learning, respond to challenges and develop across different subjects.
Predicted attainment helps secondary schools understand where pupils might perform in future assessments. Prep schools base these predictions on ongoing classroom work, internal assessments and their experience with previous cohorts.
The prep school’s relationship with secondary schools adds weight to their assessments. Admissions teams trust references from prep schools with proven track records of accurate reporting and successful pupil transitions.
